summary: Defines a SIP extension for sending geographic location information from one SIP entity to another. It supports passing location end to end and also routing decisions by intermediaries based on where the target is. It was later updated by RFC 8262 and RFC 8787.

eli5.summary: When you call for help, it is useful to tell where you are. This defines how an internet phone call carries location along, so the call can also be sent to the right place.

questions: how to send location in sip
what is the sip geolocation header

subtitle: How SIP messages carry a person's location, who may route on it, and what happens when it is bad.

tldr.problem: SIP sets up calls but had no standard way to carry the geographic location of a Target from one SIP entity to another, or to let intermediaries route a request by that location.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three header fields (Geolocation, Geolocation-Routing and Geolocation-Error) and a 424 Bad Location Information response. Location travels by value in a message body or by reference as a URI, and routing on it is off unless the sender says yes.
tldr.outcome: SIP can now convey location end to end and permit location-based routing, with privacy defaults of no. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8262 and RFC 8787.

today: RFC 6442 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 8262 and RFC 8787; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines how the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), which creates, modifies and terminates multimedia sessions, conveys the geographic location of a Target to a Location Recipient (LR). SIP acts as a Using Protocol of location information, as defined in RFC 3693.

Three new header fields are specified. Geolocation carries a reference to a Location Object (LO), Geolocation-Routing grants permission to route a request based on the location, and Geolocation-Error reports location-specific errors. The LO can be a MIME body attached to the request or a remote resource in the network.

The Target is not necessarily the sender: it could be a SIP user agent, a router, a person, or even a building. Any SIP proxy that inspects the location must also be considered a Location Recipient.
sections.eli5: The call carries a note saying where someone is. The note can be stuck to the call itself or can say where to go to look it up.

sections.title: Four Ways Location Travels
sections.content:
The RFC shows four use cases with Alice as the Target and Bob as a Location Recipient. In the first, location by value, a Location Object appears as a MIME body in the initial SIP request, directly from Alice to Bob.

In the second, location by reference, the request carries a Location URI, and Bob must dereference it at a Location Server (LS), much like content indirection in RFC 4483. The RFC notes that dereferencing may take longer than the SIP transaction timeout (Timer C for INVITE, Timer F for non-INVITE), so errors may need to travel by other means.

In the third, the request passes through a SIP intermediary (a proxy or B2BUA). Most often it just forwards the request and is not a Location Recipient, but it may use location for routing or verify it, for example for emergency calling.

In the fourth, an intermediary rejects bad location and replies with a new one, so Alice can fix the request. The RFC warns that an intermediary inserting a second location causes confusion about which to believe, and takes a "you break it, you bought it" approach: that intermediary becomes responsible for all location in the request. It does not specify how to say which location is more accurate.
sections.eli5: You can hand someone a note with your address on it, or hand them a card saying where to look your address up. A helper in the middle may pass it on, or may send it back and say, please fix this.

sections.title: The Geolocation Header Field
sections.content:
The Geolocation header holds one or more locationValue entries, each a URI in angle brackets. Allowed URI types include sip, sips, pres, http, https and cid. A cid: URI points to a MIME body part in the same message; any other scheme is a location URI to be dereferenced. GEO-URIs (RFC 5870) are not appropriate because they lack retention and retransmission flags. The header MUST have at least one locationValue, and any locationValue MUST be related to the original Target.

It is valid in INVITE, REGISTER, OPTIONS, BYE, UPDATE, INFO, MESSAGE, REFER, SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY and PUBLISH requests. An intermediary SHOULD NOT add location to a request that already has location, and SHOULD NOT modify or delete existing values. If it adds a value anyway, it MUST put it last and takes full responsibility for any 424 response about it, which it MUST NOT pass upstream.
sections.eli5: This is the label on the call that says where the location note is, either inside the same package or at an address you can visit.

sections.title: Permission to Route: Geolocation-Routing
sections.content:
The Geolocation-Routing header has two defined values, yes and no. With yes, intermediaries downstream may use the location for routing decisions. With no, they MUST NOT view an included cid: location or dereference a location URI, though UAs may still view it. A missing header means the same as Geolocation-Routing: no, and an LR MUST treat anything other than yes as no. The header MUST NOT appear more than once, and cannot have an empty value.

An intermediary without knowledge from the Rule Maker SHOULD NOT set the value to yes, since that may be more permissive than the sender intends. A no value has no special security properties; it is a request for behavior, and the request is still processed and forwarded.
sections.eli5: It is a sign on the note: may the helpers in the middle read this to choose where to send the call? If the sign is missing, the answer is no.

sections.title: The 424 Response and Geolocation-Error
sections.content:
The 424 (Bad Location Information) response rejects a request because its location was malformed, unsatisfactory or could not be dereferenced. It is a final response within a transaction and MUST NOT terminate an existing dialog. It MUST NOT be sent for a request that has no Geolocation header, and it MUST carry a Geolocation-Error header. An intermediary that wants to correct the location SHOULD put the new location in the response as a MIME body. Forwarding intermediaries MUST NOT add, modify or delete any location in a 424 response.

Geolocation-Error contains one 3-digit code and an optional code= text. Codes in the 1XX range mean the LR cannot process the location, 2XX means a permission is needed, and 3XX means dereferencing failed. An unknown specific code is treated as its top-level code (100, 200 or 300), and an unprocessable non-100 code means 100 MUST be processed. If at least one locationValue is valid, no error is sent.

To limit probing, a configurable limit on repeated rejections that coax out more location is RECOMMENDED at a maximum of three per related transaction. Dereference attempts SHOULD be limited to 10 within a few minutes, ending in a 300 error.
sections.eli5: If the note is unreadable, the receiver sends back a message saying what went wrong, using a number that says whether it is missing, forbidden, or the lookup failed. It will not keep asking forever.

sections.title: Location Profile Negotiation
sections.content:
If a request carries a location URI, the sending UA MUST also include a Supported header listing which location profiles it supports. Two option tags are defined. geolocation-sip means location can be acquired through the SIP presence event package (SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY with a PIDF-LO), for the sip, sips and pres schemes. geolocation-http means location can be acquired with an HTTP GET returning a 200 response with a PIDF-LO, for http and https. A failure to parse that response returns a Dereference Failure indication to the sender.

A recipient that does not understand the URI scheme returns the option tag as Unsupported and lists the preferred scheme's tag in Supported. New profile option tags MUST begin with geolocation followed by a dash.
sections.eli5: When you give someone an address to look something up at, you also say which ways you can be reached, like by phone or by web, so they pick one that works.

sections.title: Privacy Rules
sections.content: The RFC treats location as highly sensitive information needing protection from eavesdropping and alteration. In a SIP deployment, location may be added by the originating UA or a proxy, but in every case the Rule Maker decides who adds it and what access rules apply. How implementations honor the Rule Maker's rules, including retention and retransmission, is application specific and outside SIP operations. The RFC points to RFC 6280, RFC 4119 and RFC 5606 for guidance.
sections.eli5: Where you are is private. The person who owns the information decides who gets to add it and who may see it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Conveying location raises privacy concerns and probably authentication and integrity concerns. The RFC calls for secure mechanisms: S/MIME encryption of bodies (noted as not widely deployed), TLS for signaling, or location by reference with authenticated dereferencing. End-to-end S/MIME is a poor fit for location-based routing because proxies on the path must read the location. TLS hop by hop protects against eavesdropping in transit but exposes the data to every proxy.

By reference, each entity can be authenticated and authorized, but this needs pre-association between sender and recipient. Where it cannot be assumed, unauthenticated access MUST be permitted, and pseudorandom URIs with path encryption such as SIPS help.

A UAC MUST make location conveyance conditional on explicit user permission and MUST alert the user. There is no end-to-end integrity on a locationValue or Geolocation-Error parameter, so recipients need to trust the contents and take their own precautions.
sections.eli5: A secret note can be locked in a box, but then the helpers in the middle cannot read it. Sending only a lookup address lets you check who asks, but you must know them first.
